intro: How much of each sale actually scales with volume? Contribution margin answers that by subtracting cost of goods sold and other variable costs from revenue — fixed costs like rent or salaries stay out of it entirely.

sections.heading: How contribution margin is calculated
sections.body: Contribution Margin = (Revenue − Cost of Goods Sold − Other Variable Costs) ÷ Revenue, shown as a percentage — [the same revenue-less-all-variable-costs-divided-by-revenue shape Corporate Finance Institute uses for the contribution margin ratio](https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/accounting/contribution-margin-ratio-formula/). "Other variable costs" covers costs beyond COGS that still scale with volume — shipping, payment processing fees, sales commissions tied to each sale. This calculator computes the ratio (a percentage of revenue), not a separate dollar-amount figure, and it works from aggregate revenue and cost totals, not a per-unit price and variable cost — that per-unit version lives on the [Break-Even Point Calculator](/calculators/break-even-point) instead.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: ($100,000 − $40,000 − $8,000) ÷ $100,000 = 52.00%. Just over half of this revenue remains after the costs that scale with each sale — nothing here has touched rent, salaries, or any other fixed cost yet.

sections.heading: What contribution margin actually is
sections.body: Contribution margin is the amount remaining after the variable costs included in this calculation, before fixed costs and other expenses. It's not what the business gets to keep — fixed costs (rent, salaries, software, anything that doesn't scale directly with a sale) still have to come out of it. A 52% contribution margin means 52 cents of every revenue dollar is available to go toward covering fixed costs and, once those are covered, toward profit — not that 52 cents is profit itself.

sections.heading: Contribution margin vs. gross margin
sections.body: In this pair of calculators, [gross margin](/calculators/gross-margin) subtracts only cost of goods sold from revenue; contribution margin here subtracts COGS and other variable costs, so for the same revenue and COGS, this calculator's result is always at or below the gross margin figure. More broadly in accounting practice, the two use different cost classifications: gross margin's COGS bucket can include some costs that don't scale with volume (like factory overhead), while contribution margin is meant to isolate only costs that do — exactly which costs fall into which bucket depends on how a specific business classifies them, so treat 'contribution margin' and 'gross margin' as answering related but distinct questions, not interchangeable labels for the same number.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
items: Treating contribution margin as profit. It's revenue minus the variable costs entered here — fixed costs and other operating expenses haven't been subtracted yet, so a high contribution margin doesn't mean the business is profitable.

Using this ratio interchangeably with gross margin. They subtract different cost bases (COGS alone vs. COGS plus other variable costs here), so the two numbers answer related but different questions and shouldn't be quoted as if they were the same figure.

Including fixed costs like rent or salaries in "other variable costs." This calculator's own validation scope excludes fixed costs from that field on purpose — mixing them in overstates how much cost actually scales with revenue and understates the contribution margin.

Reading a single contribution margin percentage without checking what's in the two cost inputs. Two businesses can report the same 52% with very different cost structures behind it, depending on what each one classified as COGS versus other variable cost.

faq.a: Contribution margin is the share of revenue left after subtracting the costs that scale directly with each sale — cost of goods sold plus other variable costs like shipping or payment fees — before any fixed costs are considered. Expressed as a percentage here, it shows how much of each revenue dollar is available to help cover fixed costs and, beyond that, contribute to profit. It's a variable-cost-only view: rent, salaries, software subscriptions and other costs that don't change with sales volume are deliberately left out of this figure, which is what separates it from a full profitability measure. A business can have a strong contribution margin and still be unprofitable if its fixed costs are large enough to absorb it.

faq.q: How do you calculate contribution margin?
faq.a: Subtract cost of goods sold and other variable costs from revenue, then divide by revenue: Contribution Margin = (Revenue − COGS − Other Variable Costs) ÷ Revenue. On $100,000 in revenue with $40,000 in COGS and $8,000 in other variable costs, that's ($100,000 − $40,000 − $8,000) ÷ $100,000 = 52.00%. All three numbers need to cover the same period and the same scope of business (a single product line versus the whole company, for example) or the ratio won't describe either one accurately. "Other variable costs" should only include costs that genuinely scale with volume — fixed costs like rent or salaries don't belong in that field, since including them would understate the true contribution margin.

faq.q: What's the difference between contribution margin and gross margin?
faq.a: Gross margin subtracts only cost of goods sold from revenue. Contribution margin, as this calculator computes it, subtracts COGS and other variable costs like shipping or sales commissions, so it's always at or below the gross margin figure for the same revenue and COGS. More generally in accounting, the two rely on different cost classifications — gross margin's COGS bucket can include costs that don't scale with volume, like factory overhead, while contribution margin is meant to isolate only the costs that genuinely do. Which costs land in which bucket depends on how a specific business classifies them, so the two numbers can diverge by different amounts company to company, even when both are calculated correctly.

faq.q: Is contribution margin the same as profit?
faq.a: No. Contribution margin is the amount remaining after the variable costs included in this calculation, before fixed costs and other expenses — it says nothing about operating profit or net profit, both of which subtract fixed costs (rent, salaries, overhead) on top of variable ones. A business can post a healthy 52% contribution margin and still run at a loss if its fixed costs exceed what that margin generates in total dollar terms. Contribution margin is useful for pricing and product-mix decisions specifically because it isolates costs that respond to volume, but reading it as a profitability verdict skips the fixed-cost side of the business entirely, which is where the actual profit-or-loss answer gets decided.

faq.q: What counts as a "variable cost" in this calculator?
faq.a: Costs that scale with each unit sold or each transaction — cost of goods sold, shipping, payment processing fees, and sales commissions tied to individual sales are typical examples. This calculator's own scope excludes fixed costs like rent, salaries, or software subscriptions from the variable-cost inputs on purpose; those belong in a broader profitability calculation instead, not in contribution margin. Where a specific cost falls can vary by business — a shipping cost that's genuinely flat regardless of volume would behave more like a fixed cost, for example — so this classification depends on how a given cost actually behaves for the business entering the numbers, not a fixed universal list of what always counts as variable.
